## Introduction

How are national climate policies related to countries' political institutions, economic development, and carbon emissions? Do these relationships look different in 2000 and 2020?

In this lab, you will use data from the OECD, the World Development Indicators (WDI), and the Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) project to investigate these questions. You will use descriptive statistics, visualizations, correlation coefficients, and statistical tests to explore patterns across 34 countries.

Correlation can help identify relationships between variables, but it cannot establish that one variable causes another. For example, an association between democracy and climate-policy stringency does not demonstrate that democratic institutions cause stronger climate policies.

### Learning objectives
This lab assesses the following learning standards:

10. Derive new variables from existing ones through calculated transformations, including unit conversions, differences across time periods, and categorical dummy variables. 
21. Assess the normality of a variable and use those results to select between parametric and non-parametric statistical tests. 
25. Conduct correlation analysis across multiple variable pairs and evaluate results with respect to direction, magnitude, and significance, including changes in correlation structure across time periods or subgroups.

## 1. Load packages and inspect the data

We will use `tidyverse` for data manipulation and visualization, `Hmisc` to calculate correlation matrices, and `corrplot` to visualize those matrices.

```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(Hmisc)
library(corrplot)
library(knitr)

all_vars<-read_csv("data/climpolicy_combined.csv")
```

The combined dataset, `all_vars`, contains observations for 34 countries in 2000 and 2020. Each row represents a country in a particular year.

### Variables in the dataset

| Variable | Description |
|:--|:--|
| `country_name` | Country name |
| `country_text_id` | Country identifier |
| `year` | Observation year |
| `oecd_climpol_stringent` | OECD-derived climate-policy stringency measure |
| `co2_emissions` | Total CO₂ emissions measure |
| `gdp` | Gross domestic product (constant 2015 US dollars) |
| `tot_population` | Total population |
| `v2x_polyarchy` | V-Dem electoral democracy index |

We will also calculate GDP per capita and CO₂ emissions per capita. 

```{r}
all_vars <- all_vars %>%
  mutate(
    gdp_per_capita = gdp / tot_population,
    co2_per_capita = co2_emissions * 1e6 / tot_population
  )
```

This calculation assumes `co2_emissions` is in million tonnes and population is measured in persons. The resulting `co2_per_capita` measure is tonnes per person. GDP per capita is in 2015 US dollars, divided by population.

Inspect the new variables.

```{r}
all_vars %>%
  select(
    country_name, year, oecd_climpol_stringent,
    co2_per_capita, gdp_per_capita, v2x_polyarchy
  ) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  kable(digits = 2)
```

## 2. Explore the distributions of the variables

Before calculating correlations, examine the distributions of the variables. Correlation coefficients summarize relationships between variables, and their interpretation can be affected by skewed distributions and unusual observations.

We will focus on four measures:

- Climate-policy stringency
- CO₂ emissions per capita
- GDP per capita
- Electoral democracy

Create a subset for 2020.

```{r}
data_2020 <- all_vars %>%
  filter(year == 2020)
```

We can then create histograms to examine the distributions for each of the four variables of interest.

```{r}
data_2020 %>%
  select(
    oecd_climpol_stringent,
    co2_per_capita,
    gdp_per_capita,
    v2x_polyarchy
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 12, color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Distributions of National Characteristics, 2020",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of countries"
  )
```

The facets use different horizontal scales because the variables have different units.

You can also examine normal Q-Q plots.

```{r}
data_2020 %>%
  select(
    oecd_climpol_stringent,
    co2_per_capita,
    gdp_per_capita,
    v2x_polyarchy
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(sample = value)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Normal Q-Q Plots, 2020",
    x = "Theoretical quantiles",
    y = "Sample quantiles"
  )
```

**Task 2** _Which variables appear most skewed? Pick one of these and identify some of the countries that are outliers for this variable._

> The histograms show that the data is not normally distributed. V2x_polyarchy shows the highest skew followed by oecd_climpol_stringent.

```{r}
data_2020 %>%
  select(co2_per_capita, gdp_per_capita, oecd_climpol_stringent, v2x_polyarchy) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  summarise(W = shapiro.test(value)$statistic,
            p_value = shapiro.test(value)$p.value) %>%
  kable(digits = 3)

data_2020 %>%
  select(country_name, co2_per_capita) %>%
  arrange(desc(co2_per_capita)) %>%
  kable(digits =2, col.names = c("Country", "co2 per capita"))

```

> Based on the table, the outliers for co2 per capita are Australia, Canada, Luxembourg in the high end, and India, Brazil, and Indonesia in the lower end.

## 3. Calculate correlations for 2020

Correlation coefficients measure the direction and strength of relationships between two numerical variables. Pearson's correlation coefficient is typically used when variables are approximately normally distributed and exhibit a linear relationship, whereas Spearman's rank correlation coefficient is appropriate for non-normal or ordinal data.

**Task 3** _Select just the four variables of interest and create a correlation matrix using the appropriate measure of correlation. Print this table once you've created it._

```{r Task3}
vars_2020 <- data_2020 %>%
  select(co2_per_capita, gdp_per_capita, oecd_climpol_stringent, v2x_polyarchy)

cor_2020 <- rcorr(as.matrix(vars_2020), type = "spearman")
cor_2020
```

**Task 4** _Create a correlation plot from this matrix using `corrplot` and the parameters of your choosing_

```{r Task4}

corrplot(cor_2020$r)

```

## 4. Compare correlations between 2000 and 2020

Next, examine whether relationships between climate policy and national characteristics differ across the two years. First, we can create a new dataset for the observations in 2000.

```{r}
data_2000 <- all_vars %>%
  filter(year == 2000)
```

**Task 6** _Create a new correlation matrix for 2000 and print it, just as you did for the 2020 data. Then print both matrices so they can be compared side-by-side._

```{r Task6}
vars_2000 <- data_2000 %>%
  select(co2_per_capita, gdp_per_capita, oecd_climpol_stringent, v2x_polyarchy)

cor_2000 <- rcorr(as.matrix(vars_2000), type = "spearman")
cor_2000

corrplot(cor_2000$r)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
corrplot(cor_2000$r, title = "Spearman Correlation, 2000")
corrplot(cor_2020$r, title = "Spearman Correlation, 2020")

```

**Task 7** How did the correlation between climate-policy stringency and electoral democracy change between 2000 and 2020? What about the relationship between policy stringency and CO₂ emissions per capita?

> Correlation between climate-policy stringency and electoral democracy drastically decreases from 0.50 to 0.0026. Correlation between policy stringency and CO₂ emissions per capita increased from 0.2 to 0.26.

## 5. Examine changes within countries

Remember that these matrices describe relationships across countries within each year. A change in a correlation across years is not the same as a change experienced by an individual country. To examine changes over time, we can reshape the dataset so that each country's 2000 and 2020 observations appear in the same row.

```{r}
country_changes <- all_vars %>%
  select(
    country_text_id,
    country_name,
    year,
    oecd_climpol_stringent,
    co2_per_capita,
    gdp_per_capita,
    v2x_polyarchy
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = year,
    values_from = c(
      oecd_climpol_stringent,
      co2_per_capita,
      gdp_per_capita,
      v2x_polyarchy
    ),
    names_sep = "_"
  ) 
```
